anchor: Winnie Soon and Geoff Cox, Aesthetic Programming: A Handbook of Software Studies (Open Humanities Press, 2020; taught at Aarhus University's Digital Design programme): ten chapters, each pairing a programming concept with a critical theme and closing in a MiniX exercise with a RunMe (code) and a ReadMe (written reflection).
title: Aesthetic Programming in drag: bodies, code and debt
thesis: This course borrows its shape from Winnie Soon and Geoff Cox's Aesthetic Programming (2020): every chapter pairs one programming idea with one critical question and ends in a small work in two halves, the body you run (RunMe) and the argument you write (ReadMe). Here the work is always a body built in code, the argument is a family of that body with a prediction you write before you render it (which two will look most alike, and why), and the question is what the approximation owes. The order is the order in which you need things to make bodies. First one point that begins, resists, is held, is joined to another and leaves a trace (variable geometry). Then time and repetition turn one body into many and many vertices into a surface you can stand on (infinite loops). Then bodies come in from outside - a scan, your own tracked body, a touch - and the machine starts generating them by chance, noise, flow and rule (capture and auto-generation). Then you own a body type as a class, give it mass, balance and flesh, and let rules speak as recursion, grammar, sound and a recipe that travels (object abstraction and vocable code). Then the skin becomes data: pixels, shaders, patterns and fields (que(e)ry data). Last come the procedures that navigate, flock and learn, and the places where computation cannot close. Ada's halls are your field trips. The spine is the map you walk, but you will meet some halls earlier or later than the spine does, and each time the chapter says why.

parts.title: Getting started: variable geometry
parts.promise: You can make one point, give it a surface and a separate boundary, hold it, connect it to a second point and keep its trace, and you can say what the starter scene assumed a body is. (Aesthetic Programming ch. 1-2.)

parts.title: Infinite loops: time, repetition, surface, colour
parts.promise: Time and repetition become form: one body spins, one figure is built from parts, one becomes many, many vertices become a surface you can stand on, an index becomes a colour and a motif becomes a floor. From here every chapter ends in a family sheet with a written prediction. (AP ch. 3.)

parts.title: Capture and auto-generation
parts.promise: Bodies come in from outside (a scan, your own tracked body, a touch), then the machine starts generating them: chance with a seed, chance with a shape, noise, fields and rules. You can say what the capture takes and what the pseudo-random owes. (AP ch. 4-5; a midterm generative hall closes the part.)

parts.title: Object abstraction and vocable code
parts.promise: You own a body type as a class with exported axes (a family), give it mass, balance and flesh, then let rules speak: recursion, grammars, sound and recipes that travel between halls. (AP ch. 6-7, with The Nature of Code's Mover supplying the physics AP lacks.)

parts.title: Que(e)ry data: pixels, shaders, fields and cuts
parts.promise: A body's skin becomes data: painted pixels, shaders that answer light, a reaction-diffusion skin ported from CPU to GPU, and bodies that are fields rather than parts. (AP ch. 8.)

parts.title: Algorithmic procedures and machine unlearning
parts.promise: Procedures that navigate, flock and learn, and the places where computation cannot close: impossible bodies, entropy, bias. The final project is planned as a flowchart at the start of the part and shown in the class museum at its end. (AP ch. 9-10.)

tracks.title: Three weeks: a body family in a hall
tracks.length: 3 weeks, weekday studio. Week 1: c01, c03, c08, c09, c13 (scanning studio on the Wednesday, the scans imported and a build shared on the Friday). Week 2: c14, c16, c18, c21, and on Friday the mini-project brief as a flowchart with peer feedback. Week 3: the mini project, a guest session, optional studio kits (c10 surfaces, c17 particles, c24 soft bodies), and the showing on the last day.
tracks.mini_project: An extrapolated body (Levin and Brain's prompt, taken into VR): one body of your own written as a class with one or two exported axes (c21), with at least one scanned or sculpted element imported beside the procedural one (c13; collage after Hoch and Bellmer), placed in a hall where a body meets it - stand on it, walk through it, carry it or wear it (c14) - and shown on desktop and in the headset on the last day. RunMe: the hall and its build. ReadMe: the family sheet with the prediction written before rendering, the one-sentence claim, and debt comments in the code. The brief is drawn as a flowchart by Friday of week 2 (Aesthetic Programming ch. 9's pivot). A variant, with consent: a collective body aggregated from the class's own scans (Blas, Facial Weaponization Suite), whose family axis is the number of faces aggregated. SUPPLIED AND NAMED because the short track skips their chapters: the Day Zero project with the XR rig and pickup (XR Tools; c04), the first-person walker's movement code (c14 opens only its eye height, step and skin), the SKETCH helper (point, line, box) and segment.gd (c05), a make_surface(heights) function for the terrain (c10), a maze-floor MultiMesh helper (c12), and the kits of c02 and c05-c07, whose ideas (lifecycle, expressions, conditions, arrays, delta, basis) are explained at first use in the chapters that do run.

tracks.title: One year: the whole handbook
tracks.length: about 38 teaching weeks at one chapter a week, plus 6 pause weeks with no new code (one closing each part: returns, ports, peer critique threads); midterm after Part 3; final project c33-c38. For a 36-week year, take c36-c37 together and use two pause weeks as project weeks.
tracks.mini_project: Two projects. Midterm after Part 3 (after c20): one generative hall, Aesthetic Programming ch. 5's MiniX at room scale (at least two rules, a loop and a conditional), shown in the class museum. Final: planned in c33 as two flowchart ideas with peer review (AP ch. 9), built through c34-c37, shown in c38 as a hall in the class museum with desktop and headset builds and a 6-8 page ReadMe (AP ch. 10's length).

chapters.title: Getting started: a word that stands in the room
chapters.body: A word-body: your name as a Label3D placed on the floor of the Day Zero base scene, and the same text printed to the Output panel. Two outputs of one statement, one flat and one in space.

argument.axis: Label3D billboard mode
argument.predict: enabled and fixed_y will look most alike from a camera 45 degrees to the side and 30 degrees above: both turn toward the camera and differ only in tilt; disabled shows the word edge-on and thin.
argument.claim: A word in 3D is a flat body with a back; the billboard setting decides whether it is allowed to have one.

chapters.debt: Critique My Starter Programs (Montfort, Exploratory Programming 7-6) turned on the Day Zero base scene: what body does the prepared scene assume (a floor, a sun, a camera at standing height)? FLOW-MATIC (Marino, Critical Code Studies ch. 5): GDScript's keywords are English, so a Swedish student codes in a second language. 'Valid and intentional are different' (Montfort ch. 4): the parser checks form, not meaning.
chapters.place: Walk round the word on the desktop and find its back; then put on the headset (Day Zero's XR route) and stand behind it.
godot: planted bug: a missing colon after func _ready() - read the parser's message and its line number

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 2 (the editor, running a sketch, errors, the reference)
lineage.klee: before the point: the sheet of paper (the base scene) as a given
lineage.reference: Aesthetic Programming ch. 1 Getting started (MiniX: modify a reference example; Git; reading the reference)

chapters.project_step: Decode the Point_Zero hall's frame counter before reading any code. MiniX 1 RunMe: modify the Day Zero scene so your word stands where a visitor meets it. ReadMe: the prediction, the claim and one sentence on what the starter scene assumes. Open the Git repository where every RunMe and ReadMe of the course will live (AP's practice).

chapters.title: Variable geometry I: a point that begins and continues
chapters.body: A point (the kit's sphere) whose radius is a variable set once in _ready() and grown by a fixed amount in every _process() call: a body the engine keeps re-reading.

argument.axis: growth per frame, photographed after 120 frames
argument.predict: 0 and 0.0005 will look most alike: 120 x 0.0005 adds 0.06 m to a 0.1 m point; 0.005 gives 0.7 m and 0.05 gives a 6 m sphere that swallows the camera.
argument.claim: A body in the engine is a value the engine re-reads every frame; a small rate is invisible until time accumulates.

chapters.debt: Growth counted in frames is not time: the same script grows faster on a faster machine or a 90 Hz headset (the debt delta pays in c07). Reading: Fuller's Lexicon, 'Variable'.
chapters.place: Stand beside the point while it grows past your own height, on desktop and in the headset: at what size does a body become a room?
godot: planted bug: a variable declared inside _ready() used in _process() - 'not declared in the current scope'

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 3-4 (setup/draw: the engine calls you; variables)
lineage.klee: I.1: the point before it walks, a point that keeps a value
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 Variable geometry (variables) and ch. 3's frameCount

chapters.project_step: Decode: guess how Point_Zero's counter knows the frame. MiniX RunMe: the growing point from the point-zero kit. ReadMe: prediction, claim, and a first debt comment written into the script ('# DEBT: this grows per frame, not per second').

chapters.title: Variable geometry II: a point that resists
chapters.body: A point built in code: a MeshInstance3D with a SphereMesh for what you see, and a StaticBody3D whose CollisionShape3D is sized apart from it for what you feel.

argument.axis: collider radius as a fraction of the visible radius (a ball dropped on each point, photographed after it settles)
argument.predict: 0.5 and 1.0 will look most alike: the ball rests on the point in both, a few centimetres apart in height; 0 (the ball falls through) and 2.0 (the ball hovers in air) are the outliers.
argument.claim: What a body looks like and what it resists are two separate decisions, and the engine never makes them agree for you.

chapters.debt: Visibility and invisibility (Queer 3D's deformation list): a boundary can exceed the surface that promises it, and the ghost (seen, not felt) and the invisible wall (felt, not seen) are ordinary in games. Gaboury, Image Objects ch. 1 (Culling Vision): what is not drawn still decides. 'Valid and intentional' returns: a body with a mesh and no add_child() compiles and does not exist.
chapters.place: Stand on the point that is larger than it looks; walk through the point that has no collider.
godot: planted bug: a CollisionShape3D with no shape - read the node's configuration warning

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 1 (shapes; Zoog, a body built from primitives)
lineage.klee: I.1-I.4: the point as the start of an active line (weak)
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 Variable geometry (primitives and what a shape is made to stand for)

chapters.project_step: Decode Point_One's sun switch and point: which parts are seen, which are felt? MiniX RunMe: the resisting point from the point-one kit, with a collider you chose. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on the gap between mesh and collider.

chapters.title: Variable geometry III: an address and a frame
chapters.body: A held point: the prepared pickable body (XR Tools) with the familiar sphere, and a second point the student makes holdable; both report local and global position.

argument.axis: parent rotation about Y, the child's local position fixed at (1, 0, 0)
argument.predict: 0 and 45 degrees will look most alike: the point moves 0.77 m (a chord of the unit circle) but stays on the same side of the parent; 180 degrees puts it behind.
argument.claim: A coordinate is an address relative to someone's frame: the same three numbers name four places.

chapters.debt: Whose origin? Y-up, metres, the floor at 0 and a standing eye height are conventions the grid inherits, and the headset re-centres the origin on your body. The pickup is supplied: we see its interface, not its implementation - Chun's 'sourcery' (Programmed Visions ch. 1) is the dark spot of Ada's promise to 'reveal the black box'.
chapters.place: Carry it: pick the point up, put it down inside another frame, read local and global aloud.
godot: planted bug: $Point with a wrong path - 'Node not found'

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 14 (translation in 3D); P3D coordinates
lineage.klee: II.14 the three dimensions
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 Variable geometry (coordinates)

chapters.project_step: Decode the held point in Point_Coordinates: what does the pickup add? MiniX RunMe: make a second point holdable (standing ruling: pickup belongs here). ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment naming what the supplied pickup hides.

chapters.title: Variable geometry IV: a relation between two points
chapters.body: A measuring string between two held points: a segment stretched from a to b (segment.gd show_between() supplied) with a Label3D showing b - a and its length.

argument.axis: what moves, from one starting pose
values: A and B by +1 m in x
argument.predict: nothing, 'A and B by +1 m' and 'B rotated about A' will show the same length label while standing in three different places; only 'A by +1 m' changes the number.
argument.claim: A line is a relation: translating both ends or turning one round the other keeps it; moving one end alone changes it.

chapters.debt: A line can measure a separation without giving anyone permission to cross it (TUTORIAL_LINEAGE). distance_to() is a square root in floating point: Euclid's line is approximated. Standing ruling: distance belongs to the line, not to coordinates.
chapters.place: Stretch the string between your two hands in the headset, or walk along it on desktop.
godot: node properties set from code (position, scale)
planted bug: look_at() when a and b coincide - read the error and keep the case for c06's condition

lineage.klee: I.1: the line limited by fixed points
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 (operators)

chapters.project_step: Decode Point_Lines' line demo. MiniX RunMe: the measuring string from the point-lines kit, carried to two other objects. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what the measurement permits and forbids.

chapters.title: Variable geometry V: a trace
chapters.body: A trace: a typed Array[Vector3] that keeps the moving point's position only when it has moved further than a threshold, joined into a drawing made from movement.

argument.axis: keep threshold, one recorded hand gesture replayed
argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 will look most alike: both read as one continuous curve at room scale; 0.5 becomes a polyline of long chords.
argument.claim: A trace is a choice of what is kept: above the threshold the route stays, below it the pauses vanish.

chapters.debt: Memory as selection (Chun, 'Always Already There, or Software as Memory'): a trace preserves a route and loses its pauses. Standing rulings: the list before append, the condition before the distance threshold. Reading: Lexicon, 'Lists'.
chapters.place: Walk your own trace: retrace it with your body, then give it to a classmate to walk.
godot: planted bug: trace[trace.size()] - out of bounds

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 5 conditionals, ch. 9 arrays (mouse history)
lineage.klee: I.1 'an active line on a walk'
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 conditionals and ch. 3 arrays

chapters.project_step: Decode Point_Trace's recorder. MiniX RunMe: the trace from the point-trace kit with your own threshold. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what the trace forgets. Part 1 closes with a pause week (long track): peer feedback on six MiniX, no new code.

chapters.title: Infinite loops I: the throbber, a body that waits
chapters.body: The spinning pickup as throbber: a body that turns and bobs forever while nothing happens - rotation by speed * delta about a pivot, bobbing by interpolation.

argument.axis: pivot position (still: eight ghost copies at equal phases, a chronophotograph)
values: above the centre on the axis
argument.predict: centre and 'above on the axis' will look identical: moving a pivot along the rotation axis changes nothing; rim and outside turn spin into orbit.
argument.claim: A rotation is a relation to a pivot: a pivot on the axis leaves the body in place, a pivot off it makes the body travel.

chapters.debt: Computational time (AP ch. 3's throbber hides what the machine is doing, and cannot know when it will end - the halting problem, which returns in c36). The frame-counted growth of c02 is paid with delta. VR comfort: rotating the world under a headset makes bodies sick - comfort is not polish. Reading: Lexicon, 'Loop'.
chapters.place: Ride it: stand on a rotating platform (Trans_Introduction) on desktop, then in the headset, and note when your stomach disagrees with the pivot.
godot: planted bug: speed without delta - run at --fixed-fps 30 and 144 and read the printed angle after one second

lineage.processing: processing.org 2D Transformations (rotate, push/pop); Learning Processing ch. 14
lineage.klee: IV.33 the spinning top, a body that stands by turning (a forward glance)
lineage.reference: AP ch. 3 Infinite loops (MiniX 'Designing a throbber')

chapters.project_step: Decode the pickup in Trans_Pre: what loops, what waits? MiniX RunMe: your throbber, a body that spins while the museum loads. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what the throbber hides.

chapters.title: Variable geometry VI: a geometric body
chapters.body: A figure of primitives built by a function add_part(parent, size, pivot): limbs parented at pivots, Klee's bone, ligament and tendon, Levin and Brain's Face Generator in 3D.

argument.axis: joint hierarchy, the same 30 degrees at every joint
values: flat (all parts children of the root)
argument.predict: flat and star will look most alike: both are one level deep, so every part turns in place; the chain curls into a hook and the tree fans.
argument.claim: The same angle at every joint makes a different body depending on who is whose parent.

chapters.debt: AP ch. 2's 'Geometric emoji' and the politics of representation: whose face is the default. The default humanoid (T-pose rig, two arms, two legs, the capsule player) is Gaboury's Utah teapot (Image Objects ch. 3): which bodies are standard and who standardised them. Klee's own I.9 maps active and passive onto male and female: name it. ai_assist: ask a model for add_part and a four-limbed figure, state what must not change (the pivot convention), and write down what it assumed a body is. Reading: Lexicon, 'Function'.
chapters.place: Become it: parent the figure to the player's head and hands (a costume); on desktop it follows the camera, in the headset your hands move its arms.
godot: func add_part(parent: Node3D, size: Vector3, pivot: Vector3)
planted bug: arguments in the wrong order - read the 'Invalid argument' type error

lineage.klee: I.9 bone, ligament, tendon, muscle as passive, medial and active organs
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 MiniX 'Geometric emoji' and ch. 3 functions

chapters.project_step: Decode transform_composition_workbench in Trans_Rotation. MiniX RunMe: your geometric body, worn as a costume. ReadMe: prediction, claim, and an ai_assist log (what you asked, what you kept, what observation showed the model wrong).

chapters.title: Infinite loops II: many bodies
chapters.body: A row, then a grid, then a block of the student's pickup instanced from a PackedScene: Molnar's cube study, still regular.

argument.axis: rotation increment per index along a row of 12
argument.predict: 0 and 5 degrees will look most alike (the last cube turns 55 degrees but the row still reads as a row); 45 degrees reads as a two-beat pattern, because a cube looks the same after 90.
argument.claim: Repetition with a constant increment is already a form: the increment, not the unit, turns a row into a twist or a pattern.

chapters.debt: Klee I.6: structure is 'purely repetitive and therefore structural'. The loop is infinite until something stops it (AP ch. 3; Lexicon 'Loop'). The frame budget begins here: 10 x 10 x 10 nodes is a thousand bodies (MultiMesh answers in c12).
chapters.place: Walk through the grid as a forest of columns; stand where it thins.
godot: planted bug: adding the same instance twice - 'already has a parent'

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 6 loops (nested grid, many Zoogs)
lineage.klee: I.5-I.6 structural rhythm, the chessboard
lineage.reference: AP ch. 3 Infinite loops (for/while, arrays)

chapters.project_step: Decode molnar_cube_study in Array. MiniX RunMe: a grid of your c08 body or pickup. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what repetition makes normal.

chapters.title: Infinite loops III: faces, a surface you can stand on
chapters.body: make_face(points) -> ArrayMesh with SurfaceTool: a triangle, a fan into an n-gon, a closed polyhedron with a trimesh collider you can stand on.

argument.axis: segments of a disc or sphere (polycount), smooth normals
argument.predict: 16 and 64 will look most alike from 2 m: the gap between polygon and circle is r(1 - cos(pi/n)), 0.29 r at 4, 0.08 r at 8, 0.02 r at 16 and 0.001 r at 64.
argument.claim: A round body is a decision about how many flat faces it can afford: past about 16 segments the eye stops paying and the frame budget keeps paying.

chapters.debt: Polycount against smooth deformation, the 2023 application's own trade-off, made visible by Primitives_Ignorance's budget of smoothness and Portals' gap to the circle. Winding decides the side from which a face exists (Godot winds front faces clockwise). ai_assist returns: ask a model for the fan loop, state what must not change (clockwise winding, shared vertices) and what observation shows it wrong (the face vanishes from the front).
chapters.place: Stand on your face; walk round the open corner and the closed tetrahedron: a surface is not an enclosure.
godot: planted bug: counter-clockwise winding from generated code - the face disappears from the front; the render is the message

lineage.processing: Learning Processing ch. 14 vertex shapes (beginShape/vertex, pyramid exercise); PShape
lineage.application_wp: pre-WP, with the application's polycount vs smooth-deformation trade-off
lineage.klee: I.2-I.4 medial lines close into planes
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 beginShape/vertex

chapters.departure: Deliberate return to primitives (spine 1) after transformation and arrays: a first face needs only three points (TUTORIAL_LINEAGE), but a surface you can stand on is a loop over vertices and a function that returns a mesh, so faces come once loops exist, and the prepared primitives (Ignorance, Portals) are met as decisions the student can now rebuild.
chapters.project_step: Decode triangle_line_puzzle in Point_Triangle_Context. MiniX RunMe: a standable surface of your own. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment stating the polycount you chose and what it cost.

chapters.title: Infinite loops IV: colour by number
chapters.body: A rainbow arch of N bands (RE-DIVIDE), each band a mesh with its own StandardMaterial3D coloured by Color.from_hsv(i / N, s, v).

argument.axis: banding (declared dna axis on rainbow)
argument.predict: six and roygbiv will look most alike, one band apart; continuous (64 bands) and two are the outliers.
argument.claim: A spectrum is a decision about how many names a continuum gets; the arch changes more between two and six than between six and seven.

chapters.debt: RGB and HSV are models of one kind of eye (three cones, an sRGB screen, the headset's panel). HSV hue is not perceptual: yellow reads brighter than blue at the same value. Lerp in RGB and in HSV passes through different colours (Color_Walls). Albers: colour deceives. Reading: Lexicon, 'Pixel'.
chapters.place: Walk through the arch; let a coloured light fall on your hands (Color_Flashlight).
godot: planted bug: i / N with integers - read the 'integer division' warning, then use the debugger to see that every hue is 0

lineage.processing: processing.org Color (HSB); Learning Processing ch. 1 colour values
lineage.klee: IV.39-43 chromatic energy is Klee's ending; colour here is appearance, its energy returns in c29-c30
lineage.reference: AP ch. 2 fill and colour (AP has no colour chapter)

chapters.project_step: Decode chroma_stack in Color_Context_Placed. MiniX RunMe: colour your c09 grid by index. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on the colour model.

chapters.title: Infinite loops V: regularity, one motif and a rule
chapters.body: A walkable floor: a 4x4 motif repeated by a rule into a MultiMesh of tiles, and the same motif as an Image on a quad with UV repeat.

argument.axis: repeat rule, motif fixed
argument.predict: pm and pg will look most alike: both reflect, the glide only adds a half-tile shift on alternate rows.
argument.claim: A pattern is one motif plus a rule of repetition, and we recognise the rule before the motif.

chapters.debt: Regularity before Randomness (10 PRINT, ch. 30): the regular grid is what will make chance visible in c16. The seventeen wallpaper groups are a complete census - a closed taxonomy, and Klee II.23's non-symmetrical balance argues beyond it. Seams appear at tile edges where UVs meet in floating point.
chapters.place: Stand on the floor and walk the glide: does your step change?
godot: planted bug: use_colors set after instance_count - read the error

lineage.processing: processing.org 2D arrays, Images and Pixels, P3D textures (uv)
lineage.klee: I.5-I.6 structural repetition; II.23 non-symmetrical balance as the counter-position
lineage.reference: AP ch. 3 arrays and nested loops; 10 PRINT ch. 30 'Regularity' (AP ch. 5's reading)

chapters.project_step: Decode pattern_tile_4x4 in Pattern_Foundry. MiniX RunMe: a floor from your own motif. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what the census excludes. Part 2 closes with a pause week: ports of one earlier body (nodes to MultiMesh) and peer critique.

chapters.title: Data capture I: the scanned body
chapters.body: A body from outside: a phone or photogrammetry scan (or a Tilt Brush sculpture via Blender) imported as glTF, given a collider in code, stood beside the procedural bodies, and shipped as a desktop build.

argument.axis: decimation ratio of the imported mesh
argument.predict: 1.0 and 0.25 will look most alike at 2 m: most of a scan's triangles are smaller than a pixel there; 0.01 collapses into facets.
argument.claim: A scan's detail is mostly invisible at room distance, and its collider was never its surface.

chapters.debt: AP ch. 4 'Capture All' (datafication): a scan turns a body into data on someone's terms, and what fails to scan (dark or shiny surfaces, hair, movement [mem]) becomes a hole. Steyerl's poor image as the poor mesh. The scanned body is captured once; the procedural body can vary. Scanning people needs consent. Reading: Lexicon, 'Import/Export' (Manovich).
chapters.place: Stand the scan in your hall next to your procedural body (collage: Hoch, Bellmer) and share a build with the class the same day.
godot: planted bug: the scan arrives 100 times too big (centimetres read as metres) - print get_aabb()

lineage.application_wp: the application's polycount trade-off; Queer 3D 2024's scanning practice
lineage.klee: I.12 additive against subtractive making: a scan is neither, it is taken
lineage.reference: AP ch. 4 Data capture (MiniX 'Capture All')

chapters.departure: Import is not in the spine; it enters here as AP's Data capture because scanning is week one of Palle's Queer 3D course. It draws on primitives' polycount hall (spine 1) as a declared return.
chapters.project_step: Decode sphere_high and budget_of_smoothness in Primitives_Ignorance: how many triangles is enough? MiniX RunMe: your scan, collided and exported. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on what the scanner could not see. Share the build (Anthropy's first-chapter upload).

chapters.title: Data capture II: the captured player
chapters.body: The student's own player body: a supplied first-person walker (CharacterBody3D, Camera3D, InputMap) whose eye height and step the student sets, dressed with the c08 figure, then swapped for the XR body (skin against controller).

argument.axis: eye height, the same hall seen from the player camera
argument.predict: 1.2 and 1.6 m will look most alike: both stay under a 2.4 m lintel, so the room keeps its proportions; at 2.4 m the doorway vanishes and at 0.8 m furniture becomes architecture.
argument.claim: A room's scale is read off the height of the eye, and the default eye height is a body the software assumes.

chapters.debt: AP ch. 4 'Capture All': the headset captures head and hands 72-90 times a second. What does tracking assume - a standing height, two hands, an IPD, a body that walks (Bagnall's chapter on normativity in hardware, Queer Game Studies part III)? The capsule player is the default body (Montfort's starter critique turned on Godot's 'Squash the Creeps'). Trans_Scale: the room was scaled by four and your body did not change.
chapters.place: Become it: walk the hall at each eye height, then swap the desktop body for the XR body; the camera becomes your head.
godot: planted bug: an action name missing from the InputMap - read the 'action doesn't exist' error

lineage.klee: II.18-19 eye level and the space box seen from above or below
lineage.reference: AP ch. 4 Data capture (mouse, keyboard, webcam)

chapters.departure: Transformation halls (spine 2) after colour and tiling (4-5): AP puts data capture after infinite loops (ch. 4 after ch. 3), and the player body needs frames (c04), time (c07) and a built figure (c08) to dress it. Trans_Scale is visited here, where the student's own eye height is the subject.
chapters.project_step: Decode scale_me in Trans_Scale. MiniX RunMe: your player body at the eye height you argue for. ReadMe: prediction, claim, debt comment on the body the tracking assumes.

chapters.title: Data capture III: thresholds that notice you
chapters.body: A threshold body: a door that opens when a body enters its Area3D and reports on a world-space label who passed.

argument.predict: slide_y and slide_x will look most alike: both keep the wall's plane; swing sweeps an arc into the room.

chapters.title: Auto-generator I: chance with a seed
chapters.body: 10 PRINT as a walkable maze floor: each cell of the c12 grid gets one of two diagonal walls, chosen by a seeded RandomNumberGenerator (Schotter's grid with its order disturbed).

argument.predict: 0.1 and 0.9 will look most alike: they are mirror images, long parallel corridors running opposite ways; 0.5 is the labyrinth.
argument.claim: The maze is made by the rule's probability, not by the dice: p and 1 - p build the same labyrinth mirrored.

chapters.debt: Pseudo-randomness: a seed returns the same maze ('a pattern that returns', Random_Definition). Code-critique station (Marino's Kittler chapter as model): read the few lines of the generator behind RandomNumberGenerator and annotate what 'random' owes. AP ch. 5: control, autonomy, care; Pritchard and Soon's Recurrent Queer Imaginaries. Randomness is absent from the Bauhaus; it enters the Klee lineage with Nake's Hommage a Paul Klee (1965) as disturbance of a grid.

chapters.title: Auto-generator II: chance with a shape
chapters.body: A seeded scatter and a fountain: 200 bodies placed by a distribution law, and a GPUParticles3D emitter whose particles are born, live and die on a timer.

argument.predict: uniform and poisson-disc will look most alike: both fill the square evenly; poisson-disc only removes the clumps, which the eye may not see at 200 points.
argument.claim: Chance has a shape: the same 200 draws make a crowd, a desert or an even field depending on the law, and 'even' needs a rule against chance.

chapters.debt: The normal distribution as norm: the bell curve's 'normal' body [mem: Quetelet's average man]. Entropy (Random_Entropy: sorting lowers it; Turing and Enigma in the application). A particle's lifetime is a decision about when a body ends.

argument.predict: 30 and 110 will look most alike (irregular, holed textures); 90 is a lace of nested triangles and 250 a checkered wedge.
argument.claim: A one-byte rule decides whether the bridge is lace, checker or chaos, and reading the byte does not tell you which: you have to run it.

chapters.debt: Computational irreducibility and the edge of chaos (CA_EdgeOfChaos: flip one cell and watch the difference spread). The wrap (i + n +/- 1) % n decides that the world is a ring. chapters.title: Object abstraction III: a body that settles
chapters.body: A stacked tower and a hanging mobile composed of RigidBody3D parts and joints; a headless test decides whether each one stands.

argument.axis: centre-of-mass offset of the top stone, as a fraction of its width, 3 s after release
argument.predict: 0 and 0.1 will look most alike (both stand); the tower falls somewhere between 0.25 and 0.5, where the centre of mass leaves the support.
argument.claim: A body stands while its centre of mass stays over its support; it does not lean gradually, it falls at a threshold.

chapters.debt: The solver puts a body to sleep when it stops moving, so 'it stands' means 'the engine stopped checking'. Itten's intuition against Moholy-Nagy's claimed objectivity. Klee II.23 non-symmetrical balance: a balance of unequal parts, a queer balance rather than symmetry. A test is a prediction the machine checks.

chapters.title: Object abstraction IV: flesh, polycount against deformation
chapters.body: A jelly body: a SoftBody3D from a subdivided box, pinned at two points, its stiffness and pressure kept in a custom Resource, and baked by a @tool script into a static sculpture.

argument.predict: 8 and 16 will look most alike when sagging (smoothness saturates), while 16 costs several times the solver time of 8; 2 folds like cardboard.
argument.claim: A body can only bend where it has vertices: low polycount folds, high polycount sags like flesh, and pays in frames.

chapters.debt: The application's own question: 'the trade-off between several polygons (polycount) and the possibility of deforming a body smoothly'. Queer 3D's deformation list (speed against quality, complexity against redundancy). WP2's 'algorithmic topology of desire and the creation of queer meshes'. The planted bug makes five bodies one body: sameness as the default of shared resources.

chapters.project_step: Final project RunMe: your hall, built and exported for desktop and headset. ReadMe (6-8 pages, AP's length): the family sheet, the prediction written before the render, the claim, the debt comments collected from your code, and what your encoding hides.

learned_from: Aesthetic Programming (Soon and Cox 2020) gives the unit: one programming idea paired with one critical theme per chapter, closed by a MiniX in two halves. Ada keeps RunMe as the BODY (and its PLACE) and turns ReadMe into the ARGUMENT, but replaces AP's open reflective questions with a falsifiable PREDICTION written before the render and a one-sentence CLAIM the comparison image must support.

AP's chapter anatomy becomes the lesson rhythm: its 'Decode' (read the running work before learning the syntax) is PRIMM's Predict and Investigate done in a hall, on the hall's primary work; the syntax sections are Run and Modify on a kit; its critical essay (While()) is the DEBT step; the MiniX is Make; weekly peer feedback of about 20 minutes stays, and every RunMe and ReadMe lives in the student's Git repository from c01.

AP's order shapes the parts: geometry (P1), loops, transforms and time (P2), data capture then auto-generation (P3), object abstraction then vocable code (P4), data and pixels (P5), procedures then machine unlearning (P6). The 2020 book's own revision - generativity moved ahead of objects, reversing the 2018 course - is followed: chance (c16) comes before classes (c21).

AP's pause weeks (no new syntax) become the long track's six part-closing weeks, the place for returns and ports; AP's final project planned by flowchart two units before the end becomes c33, and its 6-8 page final ReadMe becomes c38's.

Where AP is thin for Ada, other references fill in: The Nature of Code's Mover class supplies the physics AP never teaches and justifies forces after classes (c22); 10 PRINT supplies 'Regularity before Randomness' (c12 directly before c16), the Maze Walker (c16's place) and 'Ports' (c31, CPU to shader); Montfort supplies modify-before-write (c01's MiniX), errors as a first-week topic ('valid and intentional are different') and 'Critique My Starter Programs', turned on the Day Zero scene and the capsule player.

Critical Code Studies (Marino 2020) supplies three code-critique stations at the DEBT step, never at the opening: the RNG behind Random_Definition (c16), FastNoiseLite's lattice (c18) and the marching-cubes table (c32), modelled on the Kittler chapter; the 'confessing comment' becomes a debt comment written into the student's own code every chapter; FLOW-MATIC becomes c01's note that GDScript's keywords are English.

The CCS Working Group's teaching thread supplies c21's prompt, 'describe a body in a single class', and the order write-first, critique-second inside every chapter; its code-critique thread (snippet, context, question) is the peer format for c38's exhibition.

Fuller's Software Studies: A Lexicon is used as AP uses readings: one entry pulled by each chapter's code idea (Variable, Loop, Function, Lists, Object Orientation, Import/Export, Glitch, Elegance, Pixel, Language, Copy, Interface), so theory follows the code ladder instead of running as a separate sequence.

Chun's 'sourcery' is placed where Ada first supplies a component it does not open (the XR pickup, c04), because it cuts against Ada's own promise to reveal the black box; 'Order from Order' is placed at the recipe and morphogenesis chapters (c28, c31).

Levin and Brain (Code as Creative Medium) supply body-named prompts: the Face Generator becomes c08's geometric body and the Extrapolated Body the short track's mini project; their exercise order (Unpredictability before Arrays) is further evidence for chance in the first half.
Gaboury's Image Objects supplies a critical reading at chapter grain: culling at c03, the Utah teapot at c08, object paradigms at c21, the GPU as 'procedure crystallized' at c30.

The queer and feminist sweep supplies Bagnall's normativity-in-hardware reading for the tracked player (c14), Anthropy's share-in-chapter-one (a build exported in the short track's first week, c13), Blas's collective masks as a consent-bound mini-project variant, and 'failure before futures' for the ending (c36 crisis, then c37-c38).

Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook, read in its corrected order, supplies the body book of Part I (c08's bone, ligament and tendon, with Klee's own active/passive = male/female named as a dark spot), the pendulum-to-circle-to-spiral derivation of Part IV (c27), and colour at the end as energy (c29-c30) after colour as appearance (c11).

What none of these courses has, and this candidate keeps from Ada: bodies built in code in 3D and VR, a family axis visible in a still, a prediction that can be wrong, a place where a body meets the work, and a geometric and topological queer lens (polycount against deformation, the blob, the seam) where the canon's queerness is linguistic and data-centred.
